title: 5.2.4 Lab: A random spot and colour
description: Once a second, move a coin to a random place, roll a whole-number die, and give the coin a random colour from a list.

steps.title: A random spot
steps.instructions: `draw()` already has a block that runs once a second: `if (frameCount % 60 === 0) { ... }`. Inside it, set `coin.x` to a random number from 30 to 370 and `coin.y` to a random number from 30 to 270. Run it and wait: once a second the coin should jump to a new place, always fully on the canvas.
hints: `random(min, max)` gives a number from `min` up to `max`. Decimals are fine for a position.
`coin.x = random(30, 370);` is one of the two lines. The other one is for `coin.y`.

steps.title: Roll a die
steps.instructions: Inside the same block, set `roll` to a random whole number from 1 to 6. The number shows in the top corner. Watch a dozen rolls and check that you see a 6 and never a 0 or a 7. For the first second the corner reads `roll: 0`: no roll has happened yet, so that is the starting value from `let roll = 0;` at the top. Count from the first change.
hints: `random` gives decimals, and `floor` cuts them off. Wrap one in the other.
The top number is never reached, so for 1 to 6 write `floor(random(1, 7))`. `floor(random(6)) + 1` also works.

steps.title: A random colour
steps.instructions: Inside the same block, pick a random position in the `colors` list: a whole number from 0 up to the last position. Then set `coin.color` to the colour at that position. Use the list's `.length` so the line keeps working if a colour is added.
hints: `colors.length` is how many colours there are. Five colours means the positions are 0 to 4.
`const pick = floor(random(colors.length));` gives the position, and `colors[pick]` reads the colour there.

requirements.title: The coin gets a random x
requirements.description: The x position comes from random(...), straight on the line or through a variable first. Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)

requirements.title: The coin gets a random y
requirements.description: The y position comes from random(...), straight on the line or through a variable first. Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)

requirements.title: The die is a whole number from 1 to 6
requirements.description: random is wrapped in floor (or int) and shifted so the answers run 1 to 6; a round() of random(1, 6) also counts. Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)
requirements.hint: The top of random(1, 7) is never reached, so floor of it is 1 to 6.

requirements.title: A random position in the colors list
requirements.description: A whole number from 0 to the list's last position is chosen at random, using the list's length. Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)
requirements.hint: floor(random(colors.length)) is a whole number from 0 to 4.

requirements.title: The coin takes the chosen colour
requirements.description: coin.color is set from the colors list. Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)
requirements.hint: colors[pick] reads the colour at that position. Assign it to coin.color.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote a moSHion sketch (p5-style JavaScript with a physics world) for the lab "5.2.4 Lab: A random spot and colour". The task they were given: draw() already has a block that runs once a second, an if that tests frameCount % 60 === 0. Inside it: set coin.x to a random number from 30 to 370 and coin.y to a random number from 30 to 270, so the coin jumps somewhere new but stays fully on the 400 by 300 canvas; set roll to a random whole number from 1 to 6 (it is shown in the corner); and pick a random position in the colors list (a whole number from 0 up to the last position, using the list's .length so it keeps working if a colour is added), then set coin.color to the colour at that position. What the starter file already had: the canvas, the coin, a five-colour list called colors, roll starting at 0, the text that shows roll, and the empty once-a-second block with step comments. The starter meets none of the criteria. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do when the sketch runs. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, if / else chains or ternaries, helper functions, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment or inside a string never runs, so a line the student only wrote in a comment does not count. moSHion facts that matter here: random(a, b) gives a decimal from a up to, but never reaching, b; random(n) gives a decimal from 0 up to n; random(list) gives one item of the list. floor() (also int() and Math.floor()) drops the decimal part, rounding down. Math.random() gives a decimal from 0 up to 1. The positions in a list start at 0, so a five-item list has positions 0 to 4 and its .length is 5. frameCount % 60 === 0 is true once every 60 frames, which is once a second. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise. Write for a 14-year-old reader: short sentences and plain, everyday words.

rubric.title: The coin gets a random x
rubric.description: coin.x is set from random(...) (or Math.random()), on the same line or through a variable first, or the coin is made at a random x. The lab asks for 30 to 370 so the coin stays fully on the canvas; any range that keeps it on the 400-wide canvas counts. Setting it outside the once-a-second block still counts for this card (the coin just jumps every frame). Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)

rubric.title: The coin gets a random y
rubric.description: coin.y is set from random(...) (or Math.random()), on the same line or through a variable first, or the coin is made at a random y. The lab asks for 30 to 270 so the coin stays fully on the canvas; any range that keeps it on the 300-tall canvas counts. Setting it outside the once-a-second block still counts for this card. Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)

rubric.title: The die is a whole number from 1 to 6
rubric.description: roll is set to a random whole number whose smallest possible value is 1 and largest is 6: a random number with its decimal dropped by floor (or int, Math.floor), and a range or a + 1 that makes it start at 1. Remember the top of random(a, b) is never reached. A round() of a random number from 1 to 6 also stays inside 1 to 6 and counts. Not met: a decimal with nothing dropping the decimal part, a range that can give 0 or 7, or a range that can never give 6. Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)

rubric.title: A random position in the colors list
rubric.description: A whole number from 0 up to the list's last position is picked at random using the list's .length (a random number up to the length with its decimal dropped), so it keeps working if a colour is added. Picking an item straight from the list with random(colors) also counts. Not met: a pick that can never reach the first or the last colour, a position with a decimal part, or no randomness. A fixed 5 in place of the length picks correctly today, but the step asks for the list's length: mark that partial and say why. Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)

rubric.title: The coin takes the chosen colour
rubric.description: coin.color is set to an item of the colors list: read with square brackets and a position (a variable or an expression), or picked with random(colors). Setting one fixed colour is not met. Help: 5.2.2 (Reading: Random numbers and timers)
